Strictly speaking, it’s not even discounted, but its already cheap $35 price tag means this is just too good to pass up.

    Recent findings suggest that the SlideTag is a tiny digital photo frame that sits on a keychain, but it’s also a tracker compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub. You can load it up with photos and have the six-color E-Ink display cycle through them at set intervals, or you can put something more practical on the screen.

    The Kodak app makes it easy to generate a QR code, display a to-do list, countdown to a special event or just show you the current date in a nice calendar display. It’s incredibly easy to use, the color E-Ink display is surprisingly good and setting up the tracking feature is super easy. This thing does exactly what it states it does, and with very little learning curve.

    So what’s the catch? You don’t really get to choose what the outside of your SlideTag looks like. These clever little photo frames are only available as a blind box, showcasing eight designs across the vibrant history of Kodak’s packaging and something Kodak calls a secret edition, which is unique to this set.

    I ordered two, and while both designs I found in the packaging are great, there are other designs in the lineup I’d have chosen first. Some retailers are selling cases of eight SlideTags with promotional packaging, like you’d see at the checkout counter of a grocery store, but this case doesn’t guarantee you’re going to get all eight designs. There’s no real way to know what you’re going to get.

    That level of risk may not be your thing, but if you’re looking for a way to add a stealthy little tracker with no shortage of personality to your bag, backpack or purse, I think this is a great option. It also makes a great little gift, perfect for a stocking or white elephant party. And if this level of cutesy fun isn’t your thing, Apple’s second-gen AirTags are on sale for $18 this week.

    Latest Update: What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car.
    • The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:.
    • Sources indicate that A visual exterior inspection.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

    The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:.

    Sources indicate that A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

    An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

    According to recent reports, A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

    Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic concerns that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

    Recent findings suggest that inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

    According to recent reports, detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

    Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

    The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

    However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

    All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

    Sources indicate that some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

    However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

    In a recent development, some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

    Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

    Reddit people are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

    It has been revealed that car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

    Addas a preferred source on Google.

    Regulatory resets and institutional funding pullbacks across China are pressuring the industry. FinVolution holds RMB 8.4 billion in cash and short-term investments to navigate the turbulence.

    Financial stability rests on a historical low leverage ratio, calculated as risk-bearing loan balance divided by equity, of 1.5 times. Management continues to prioritize loan quality heading into the fourth quarter.

    #222885. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (744 w)

    What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
    • Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the manufacturer.
    • Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

    Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the manufacturer. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

    Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

    "Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate fresh multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider remarked in a note Thursday.

    The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

    Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

    On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

    According to recent reports, tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

    It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The tech giant had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

    It has been revealed that neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

    Recent findings suggest that coreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

    It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

    "We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he noted.

    "However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

    CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person.".

    In a recent development, "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my manufacturer every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us.".

    Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any significant changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

    The real issue is just how much money the organization will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

    In a recent development, "Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies.".

    — CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

    What Are Repositioning Cruises?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another.
    • Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.
    • Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

    Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

    Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

    It has been revealed that one key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

    This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

    According to recent reports, another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

    According to recent reports, just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

    It has been revealed that repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit crucial sites when off the ship.

    Sources indicate that if there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

    For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy demonstrates, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

    In a recent development, many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

    Sources indicate that if you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

    You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

    Recent findings suggest that keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

    Industry observers note that here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

    Industry observers note that this journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

    Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between Newly introduced York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

    Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

    Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

    If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

    Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching Newly introduced York.

This is 25 basis points lower than yesterday and unchanged from a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

    Recent findings suggest that the amount of day-to-day discrepancy we've been seeing prompted me to take a little cruise around the web this morning to see what 30-year rates lenders are advertising. Mortgage lenders' rates are never identical, but when we're seeing rapid change, the gaps between lenders tend to widen — and that's for sure what I saw. I looked at six different lenders, and saw a nearly 70-basis-point difference between the highest and lowest APRs. (And yes, that was looking for the same loan amount, location and so on.).

    My point is, whether you're looking to buy or refinance, make sure to shop multiple lenders. You're the same candidate bringing the same financials to each one, but you could end up with extremely different rate quotes. And it pays to compare. Freddie Mac estimates that comparing at least two lenders could save you up to $600 per year in interest. Compare four or more, and that savings is over $1,200 annually.

    Mortgage rates may be lower today, but like I mentioned above, it's been more of a seesaw than a ski slope — and we may be about to hit the high side again. The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out tomorrow morning. Recently, when rates have moved higher, inflation's been in the mix.

    Industry observers note that strong inflation's generally bad for borrowing, including to buy a home, because higher interest rates are the remedy. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers of the Federal Reserve actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation. While the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions.

    Industry observers note that we already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three significant inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI indicated wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

    Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out tomorrow morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

    Markets are right now anticipating a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting. Even though that'll remain the most likely outcome, a poor showing from PCE could spark speculation about a half-point hike. That probably won't be good for mortgage rates.

    But back to the upcoming holiday: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week.     How to Get Grants for College

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education.
    • Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses.
    • Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

    Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

    Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

    There are four main types of grants:.

    Federal grants come from the federal government.

    State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

    Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

    Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

    Industry observers note that to receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

    Recent findings suggest that federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

    Recent findings suggest that some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

    In a recent development, after you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

    According to recent reports, most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal strategy.

    In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

    If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

    Recent findings suggest that grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

    In a recent development, some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

    Expenses grants aren’t meant for:.

    Recent findings suggest that after your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment aims, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

    Industry observers note that to maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

    Recent findings suggest that your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

    Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

    Industry observers note that you don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

    If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:.

    You withdrew from your program.

    You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

    It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

    In a recent development, if you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

    Sources indicate that grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By James Halley – Nov 27, 2026 at 7:55AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than UnitedHealth Group ›.

    Industry observers note that unitedHealth Group (UNH +1.75%) recently upgraded its yearly earnings guidance for the third time this year. In each of its quarterly earnings reports, its expectations for yearly adjusted earnings per share (EPS) have climbed.

    It has been revealed that in its 2025 annual report, the healthcare insurer had 2026 adjusted EPS of at least $17.75. After the first quarter, it stated it would be at least $18.25. The second quarter brought another increase to between $19.50 and $20. Now, after the third quarter, UnitedHealth Group is predicting full-year EPS of at least $20.50.

    According to recent reports, in the meantime, though, the stock has climbed only 3%. So far this month, its shares are down more than 18%. That's because of a rising chorus from both sides of the political aisle that something must be done to rein in Medicare Advantage costs, and because of the possibility that Medicare-for-all proposals, if they became law, would upend the company's business model.

    In a recent development, on Nov. 16, a proposed rule, called CRUSH, from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), was floated to curb healthcare fraud. This heightened concerns about increased expenses and potential repayment liabilities for Medicare Advantage providers such as UnitedHealth Group. The rule would increase audits of insurance providers and allow CMS to recover improper payments.

    The current dip for UnitedHealth Group presents an opportunity and a question: What would a $10,000 investment return if the manufacturer's turnaround continues?

    In a recent development, if you had invested $10,000 in UnitedHealth Group stock 10 years ago and reinvested its dividends, you would have around $26,600 today, representing an annual return of 10.3%. Over the next 10 years, it's possible the stock could deliver an annual return of more than 10%. Let's make the case for why that could happen.

    NYSE · As of 10:44 AM ET 11/27/26.

    The stock is trading at around 19 times trailing earnings, well below its historical valuation of about 22 times earnings.

    In a recent development, after a couple of down years, the company appears to be in the midst of a turnaround. It saw quarterly EPS rise by 76.21% year over year in Q3 and by 61.72% in Q2. It has been able to do that because management's margin-over-volume strategy of exiting unprofitable geographies, tightening benefits, and shifting Medicare Advantage mix toward higher-margin Special Needs Looks (SNPs) is successfully restoring core insurance margins.

    In Q3, UnitedHealth Group reported that revenue declined year over year by 0.09% to $86.3 billion. However, net income rose to $2.8 billion, up from $1.8 billion in the same period a year ago, and nine-month operating margin rose from 5.6% to 7%.

    Sources indicate that most headline-grabbing CMS rules are proposed regulations subject to public comment periods, revisions, and multi-year phase-ins rather than instant earnings hits. For example, key provider enrollment provisions under the CRUSH proposal would not take effect until the blueprint year beginning two years after a final rule is published.

    Plus, UnitedHealthcare intends reprice annually, allowing the company to adapt to changes. If CMS reduces benchmark reimbursements or tightens quality bonus thresholds, UnitedHealthcare adjusts by trimming supplemental benefits (such as dental, vision, or over-the-counter allowances), raising deductibles, or narrowing provider networks, as it did for its 2027 bids to protect its 2% to 4% Medicare Advantage operating margin target.

    Heavy compliance burdens, stricter risk-adjustment documentation rules, and narrower margins disproportionately squeeze smaller regional insurers and start-up prepares that lack massive actuarial, legal, and data infrastructure.

    When tighter rules force smaller competitors to exit unprofitable counties or slash benefits, UnitedHealth's unmatched scale allows it to absorb compliance costs and capture displaced market share over time.

    Industry observers note that even if Medicare Advantage faces strict federal scrutiny, UnitedHealth Group is not a pure-play Medicare Advantage insurer. Its earnings are heavily cushioned by Optum (Optum Rx, Optum Health, and Optum Insight) and by its massive commercial employer-sponsored insurance book, insulating overall enterprise earnings from single-program rule changes.

    Recent findings suggest that the company raised its quarterly dividend by just under 5% this year to $2.32 per share, the 17th consecutive year it has increased its dividend. The dividend yield is an above-average 2.65%.

    If UnitedHealth Group can sustain double-digit EPS growth, the stock would likely grow by 12% to 15% each year. Counting the tech giant's dividend, it wouldn't be unreasonable for a $10,000 investment now to be worth at least $31,058 a decade from now.

    The tech giant has faced challenges to its business models before, but its size and scope give it the ability to overcome legal challenges that could affect its bottom line, potentially widening its moat against competitors.

    It has been revealed that nvidia (NVDA -0.90%) stock has raced higher during most of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and this is thanks to the firm's leading position in the space. This continued in the third quarter, as revenue jumped more than 100% to $115 billion and the tech giant generated high profitability on sales with a gross margin of more than 74%.

    You might expect such a stock to be expensive, but Nvidia, due to recent headwinds, has actually seen its valuation tumble to record lows. At today's levels, is Nvidia a screaming buy or a value trap? Let's find out.

    First, you might wonder how high-growth Nvidia could today have a valuation that puts it in the category of "value stock." Nvidia trades for only 16x forward earnings estimates, a historically low level for this tech player.

    NVDA PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

    Industry observers note that A few elements have contributed to this. Throughout this year, investors have worried about major tech companies' spending levels as they lead the AI infrastructure build-out. Players such as Amazon and Alphabet, for example, are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers, chips, and more to serve AI demand. But investors question whether this enormous investment will match the future revenue opportunity. This has hurt AI stocks at times in 2026, and broader economic concerns amid rising inflation have also proved challenging.

    According to recent reports, to make matters worse, just recently, reports emerged that Nvidia chief Jensen Huang allegedly had affairs with at least two women -- one called a Chinese spy by U.S. intelligence agents and the other an Nvidia executive. Huang stepped down, and the stock plummeted. Nvidia's board reinstated him days later, and the stock rebounded, but it continues to trade at a dirt cheap valuation.

    Industry observers note that now, let's consider our question: Is Nvidia a screaming buy or a value trap? For a stock to be a value trap, the company must have a significant amount of underlying trouble that is putting pressure on or will put pressure on earnings. This could be declining market share or a sustained drop in revenue, for example.

    Industry observers note that nvidia isn't in this situation. To the contrary, business is booming. In the latest quarter, revenue and profit advanced in the triple digits to record levels, and the tech giant's rollout of its latest platform, Vera Rubin, met with soaring demand. Meanwhile, Nvidia's multi-year road map and its commitment to innovation offer us reason to be confident in its competitive position.

    Recent findings suggest that so, the stock isn't a value trap. Instead, it's declined due to the headwinds I mentioned above -- and the pressure remains. Some investors continue to worry about AI spending, and any slowdown in such spending could impact the revenue growth of Nvidia and peers.

    Industry observers note that nvidia-specific troubles also remain in the background. The company's board is investigating Huang's interactions with the woman whom intelligence agents consider a spy. Separately, Huang must testify before Congressional panels early next month on the matter. Meanwhile, the press also reported recently that regulators are investigating Nvidia's accounting practices. All of these elements could weigh on stock performance in the weeks and months to come.

    Recent findings suggest that now, we know Nvidia isn't a value trap -- but is it a screaming buy? It's clear that the stock looks like a bargain today considering the manufacturer's earnings track record and potential earnings down the road. That said, any negative news stemming from the headwinds I mentioned above could slow Nvidia's growth story at least temporarily. Amid the uncertainty, Nvidia isn't the best bet for a cautious investor today, and this uncertainty means that it isn't yet a "screaming" buy.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

    Recent findings suggest that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

    Industry observers note that inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

    Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

    P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

    » Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

    In a recent development, mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to latest inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

    It has been revealed that like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

    It has been revealed that here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

    The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

    It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

    Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

    The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

    It has been revealed that this AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

    That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

    It has been revealed that let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

    In a recent development, next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

    In a recent development, on Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

    The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the substantial one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

    Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

    According to recent reports, what we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

    Recent findings suggest that if we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

    Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

    10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF ›.

    Recent findings suggest that 2026 has been challenging for stock market investors. The diversified S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.23%) index and the technology-heavy Nasdaq-100 index generated strong returns through the first nine months of the year, only to shed most of those gains since October. In fact, the Nasdaq-100 was recently down by more than 20% from its peak on an intraday basis.

    Industry observers note that with rising interest rates and turbulence in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry casting a cloud of uncertainty over the market, being diversified heading into 2027 might be a smart strategy. The Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI +1.29%) is one of the most diversified exchange-traded funds (ETFs) money can buy, because it tracks the Morningstar U.S. Total Market index, which holds all 3,463 companies listed on American stock exchanges.

    That means the ETF has exposure to tech giants like Nvidia and Amazon, alongside small-cap growth stocks like DigitalOcean and Duolingo. Here's why it could be a great buy for the new year.

    According to recent reports, the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF is weighted by market capitalization, meaning the most valuable companies in the fund have a much greater influence over its performance than the least valuable. Therefore, its top five holdings also happen to be the largest companies in the U.S. (and the world): Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet.

    In a recent development, those five companies have a combined market cap of $18.7 trillion, so they represent 25.9% of the value of the Vanguard ETF's entire portfolio. That sounds like a very high weighting for an ETF that holds almost 3,500 different stocks, but those five giants have even bigger weightings of 29.2% in the S&P 500 and 50.1% in the Nasdaq-100.

    Its lesser exposure to those tech powerhouses is the primary reason why the Vanguard ETF typically underperforms the S&P and Nasdaq-100 over the long term.

    However, its high level of diversification also means the Vanguard ETF tends to suffer shallower declines during volatile periods. For example, while the Nasdaq-100 was recently down by as much as 20% from its peak, the Vanguard ETF was down by just 11.5% at its lowest point.

    It has been revealed that there is another benefit to being highly diversified. The Vanguard ETF gives investors exposure to thousands of small- and mid-cap companies that aren't present in the major indexes. Here are some examples:.

    Recent findings suggest that the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF has delivered a compound annual return of 9.4% since it was established in 2001. However, thanks to the incredible growth in the technology sector, it has delivered a much faster annual return of 23.1% over the last three years.

    NYSEMKT · As of 10:43 AM ET 11/27/26.

    Therefore, while its long-term returns tend to be relatively modest, the ETF is certainly capable of delivering accelerated gains in certain conditions. But even if we assume the fund delivers a compound annual return of just 9.4% going forward, that's still enough to help investors build life-changing wealth.

    As I highlighted earlier, those returns are likely to come with lower volatility compared to what investors might experience in larger indexes like the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq-100. That alone is an attractive proposition as we head into an uncertain 2027.

    Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some newly introduced money goals and make progress toward them.
    • That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.
    • Recent findings suggest that “You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some newly introduced money goals and make progress toward them.

    That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

    Recent findings suggest that “You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”.

    One important component of the Great Lock In is developing upcoming routines that will last well into 2027, notes Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

    “We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he claims. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”.

    In a recent development, ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

    Sources indicate that what’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

    Recent findings suggest that “Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird notes. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”.

    Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman indicates.

    If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the upcoming saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

    “It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

    Once you’ve outlined those major goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird indicates.

    Industry observers note that he suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

    Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he states.

    Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird indicates.

    Industry observers note that “Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he indicates. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

    Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

    Sources indicate that baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

    Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he claims. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”.

    Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

    Sources indicate that with credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird claims. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.).

    Sources indicate that “High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman states. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

    It has been revealed that even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

    “It’s like a diet,” Baird notes. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”.

    “Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he indicates.

    Industry observers note that in fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he indicates. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”.

    4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
    • Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
    • In a recent development, but what about your money?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

    Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

    In a recent development, but what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

    Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

    According to recent reports, don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

    In a recent development, last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

    It has been revealed that if systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, said Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good proposal, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

    “My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson stated. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

    According to recent reports, if your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

    “This is the step I push hardest,” Judge says. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

    If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

    Recent findings suggest that make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

    Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

    Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

    Recent findings suggest that take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

    Recent findings suggest that and set a reminder to enhancement your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the big concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he says. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

    It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

    “The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” mentioned Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).
    • Industry observers note that is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in?
    • It has been revealed that first, let's remember how we got here.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).

    Industry observers note that is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

    It has been revealed that first, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

    The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

    Sources indicate that zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:.

    This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

    For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

    Sources indicate that the following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

    Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

    The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

    According to recent reports, the major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

    That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

    One notable clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

    In a recent development, any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

    We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

    The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

    In a recent development, from here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 8:36AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Noah ›.

    On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 24, 2026, Noah Holdings (NOAH -5.79%) reported net revenue of 509 million renminbi (RMB), the official currency of China, and outlined an operational shift toward an open global wealth management platform. Fresh cross-border regulatory rules in China forced the company to restructure how it acquires wealth-management clients and distributes products overseas. Understanding this platform pivot reveals how the business prepares to grow recurring fees outside its home market. Three things management noted stand out.

    China's regulatory changes created short-term revenue disruption, prompting the company to replace traditional relationship managers (RMs) -- client-facing wealth advisors -- with digital tools and external partner networks. Nontraditional channels now drive most latest client accounts in Hong Kong and Singapore.

    In a recent development, restructuring Mainland operations triggered 35 million RMB in one-time employee severance costs, dragging down operating profit. Strong liquidity and zero debt give the business plenty of runway to absorb restructuring expenses without straining operations.

    Entering fresh geographic markets historically required hiring large teams of local wealth advisors, creating heavy fixed cost structures. Management's new expansion strategy relies on artificial intelligence (AI) systems to handle client onboarding and daily operations, keeping regional footprints lean.

    According to recent reports, international expansion momentum is building as client account activations accelerate, and management isn't hiding its satisfaction with overseas performance. The tech giant holds key structural advantages, including established licensing in Singapore and Hong Kong, an open partner framework, and a clean balance sheet. Management is watching recurring management fees -- the steady service charges collected on managed assets -- to confirm that international growth offsets shrinking legacy private equity pools.

    Long-term value depends on whether the organization can successfully scale its digital client service model across new markets in Asia and the West.

    Sources indicate that on its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 19, 2026, ClearSign (CLIR -3.45%) announced a gross margin expansion to 55.6%, up from 35.8% in the prior-year period. The manufacturer relies on an asset-light strategy that focuses on intellectual property (IP), or proprietary technology designs, rather than high-cost manufacturing. Three things management noted stand out.

    ClearSign expanded gross margins by granting fabrication rights to an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) that builds equipment under license, enabling the business to earn licensing fees without incurring hardware assembly costs.

    Refineries require field data from Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems (CEMS), which stream stack measurements to regulators, before committing capital to replace legacy pollution control equipment.

    ClearSign standardizes engineering designs for midstream gas-processing burners, which cut turnaround times and enable repeatable volume across West Texas gas fields.

    Field deployments at major oil facilities are advancing, shifting focus from initial development to commercial execution. Management says computer modeling gives ClearSign a design edge by bypassing physical testing cycles, while management watches project execution and proposal conversion.

    Scaling through verified site references remains the central path to reaching break-even volume, which management has pegged at about 160 burners a year.

    #222839. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (625 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct.
    • However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive.
    • In a recent development, buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

    However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the organization's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

    In a recent development, buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

    This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

    This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

    By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.
